findings.where: The 'Get Mark's briefings on PPP reform' band directly below the hero, at both widths
findings.fault: House blue is used here as a full-width section ground. The page's own palette gives blue only these jobs: the first-screen action, the wordmark, links and the curve. So the blue is doing two jobs at once. The email box was the one blue thing on the first screen, and now it has to compete with a larger, louder blue field just below it. On the phone the band starts right where the hero ends, so the first scroll goes from slate straight into saturated blue. That breaks the direction card's 'page below in grey on warm white' and its 'one quiet contact'.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who judges the first screen first and asked v7 for one quiet contact with the page below in grey on warm white. A development-bank officer would see two loud calls to action fighting each other, which tips the page toward the 'salesy' look the research warns against.

findings.where: The PDF card ('Streamlining the PPP Process…') at the end of the article specimen, at both widths
findings.fault: This is the one resting element that gets four treatments together: a pale blue tint that is not in the palette, a blue 1 px border, a wide soft drop shadow and rounded corners. Everything else on the page has square corners, no shadow and no fill: the swatches, the email box, the Subscribe button and the motion thumbnail. A strong border, a fill and a wide shadow on one resting element is the combination the surface rules forbid. Next to the flat, paper-like page around it, the card looks like an app widget.
findings.who_objects: The founder and Mark. The research says the PDF list 'is the product', and here it looks like it was pasted in from a SaaS template rather than set like the legal-journal page around it. Angélique will copy this card for every new PDF, so the mismatch will spread.

findings.where: Hero photograph of Mark (desktop first screen, phone first screen, the motion-sketch thumbnail)
findings.fault: The grade does not tint the photograph into the house blue-grey. It keys out the backdrop and replaces it with a flat slate fill, so Mark appears as a hard-edged cut-out on a flat colour card, with no light or depth behind him. This comes from the candidate's own SVG filter, which every future photograph will also go through, not from the stand-in photo.
findings.who_objects: The founder, who asked for a full-bleed photograph graded into the house colours with 'real people in real light' (Kümmerlein, Cornerstone). A cut-out headshot on flat colour looks like a stock corporate bio, which is the look the personal-advisor test fails.

findings.where: The 'PALETTE' section label and the blue numerals of the article's numbered list
findings.fault: The page states its own rule, 'blue only where something can be clicked', but sets static text in link blue. The parts map lists 'PALETTE' as static in a link's colour, and the list numerals are static too. 'PALETTE' is also the only section label in blue; 'Type pair', 'An article page' and 'Motion sketch' are in grey. So like labels are coloured differently.
findings.who_objects: A reader who has learned that blue means a link and then finds blue words that do nothing. Angélique, who has no consistent rule to follow when she adds a section label.
